scope: Inventory and lexical guard backed by full manual source review (V04 phase F); not a theorem prover or semantic detector for arbitrary English. It enforces that every tier-A statement in a region has one reviewed disposition and that named evidence exists; it does not establish that a claim is true.
limits: A claim phrased without tier-A vocabulary is not seen; the vocabulary is the list below. A forbidden phrase is a regex: a phrasing it does not match is not seen. Rule 5 (memory-saving claims) covers the forms in its fixture table (fixtures.fail); other phrasings are an accepted limit. Rule 5 treats a claim as hedged only when the hedge (not/never measured, verified, established, claimed or promised; unverified) immediately follows it and ends its sentence, in parentheses or as the clause's final words (optionally followed by "here" or "in this repository"); such an explicitly unverified claim passes.

Matching uses escape-neutralized text: in every statement, Swift escapes (\n, \t, \r, \0 → space; \", \', \\ → the character; \u{hex} → the character; a backslash followed by whitespace, a multi-line literal's line continuation, joins the next line) are replaced before the vocabulary, the forbidden phrases and tombstone phrases are matched, so "\nMemory savings: 50%" is seen; fingerprints stay on the raw normalized text.
Symbols are names, not signatures: moving a statement between overloads with one name is not detected.
#if branches are not evaluated and regex literals are not lexed.
adjacent-invariant and unverified-contract reasoning is reviewed text; only its presence and wording are checked.
A named test supports its claim only within that test's fixtures; whether it runs is shown by the suite run.
Q17 sites are recorded weak-consumption observation bodies; they are never performance evidence.

Reads: the ledger, the region files (Swift and Markdown), the evidence files (named tests, body pins, flag tests, dated artifacts), every Swift file matched by a forbidden-phrase path or a caller-inventory glob (today: every Swift file under Sources/, Tests/ and Benchmarks/), the Markdown files named as literal forbidden-phrase paths (today README.md, CHANGELOG.md and the 13 maintained documents under Docs/), and the recorded-site files.

excludeLiterals admits only pure identifiers: segments joined by '.' or '-', each a word starting with a letter or '_' (interpolations allowed after the first character), a lone interpolation, a decimal integer, or a hex digest of 16+ digits. Numeric-unit literals such as "50%", "10-20%", "3x-faster" and "\(n)x" are statements. A literal that matches any forbidden phrase ("lock-free", "auto-prefetch", "zero-copy") is never excluded. A tier-A word in a pure-identifier literal that matches no forbidden phrase ("optimized" in a case ID) stays excluded: 63 region literals at T13 phase 2 (a count recorded by review; nothing re-counts it).

Forbidden-phrase paths are literal file paths (no *, ? or [) or fnmatch globs; paths must be non-empty and every path must match at least one file (R8). A pattern with an anchor (^, $, \A, \Z) or a lookaround carries a keyword screen; every rule carries fixtures.fail (and may carry fixtures.pass): each must-fail fixture must match the pattern and pass the screen, and each must-pass fixture must not match (R8). An exemption names a path, a fingerprint, an owner and a reason, and must still match a present statement.

R3 matches only the method part of path::Suite.method: a citation that loses its suite qualifier still passes. Comparisons between references (R8 overlap, body pins) use the resolved identity (path, enclosing type, method), so path::method and path::Suite.method of one test are the same test.

R5 wording list: "not verified", "unverified", "not established", "not promised", "no ... guarantee". For a string literal (runtime text) the wording may instead sit in ONE SENTENCE of its adjacent comment block (comment lines directly above, a trailing comment, the doc of the nearest enclosing named declaration) that also names Q11 or says runtime/returned/printed followed by text, string(s), output or note(s).

Q14 counts words in comment- and literal-masked code: uses outside the defining file per file (callers) and inside it, declaration included (definedInOccurrences). A homonym counts as a use, so reviewed homonyms are recorded.

evidence.bodyPin (a drift guard that hashes the source a note was written from) and evidence.flagTests (tests that check a record field the note relates to) are traceability only: they must resolve (R8) and are never evidence for the statement. A test named in any bodyPin may be named-test evidence only for an entry listed in bodyPinDescribers (R8).

Markdown files are read only when named as a region or as a literal forbidden-phrase path; a glob path selects Swift files only. Inline Markdown (emphasis, code spans, links) is kept in the statement text, so it is part of the fingerprint.

Rule 6 (numeric performance claims in Docs/Performance_Guide.md and README.md) is sentence-scoped: a sentence ends at ., ! or ? followed by whitespace, and a claim passes only when its own sentence contains "not verified", "unverified", "not measured", "not established" or "not promised", or a path under Benchmarks/, Docs/, Tests/ or Scripts/ ending in .md, .json, .csv or .txt (the path is not checked to exist). Its forms are its fixture table: a time in ns or µs (or ~N ms), an N x / N× multiplier not followed by a number, "N times faster/slower" and "N% faster/slower/speedup/improvement", and (T13 RD3) the spelled-out forms "twice/thrice/half as fast" or "the speed/throughput/time", "<number word or N> times faster/as fast", "N-fold/threefold" with a speed word, "orders of magnitude faster/more/...", "faster/speedup/improve/reduce ... an order of magnitude", "N percent/per cent faster or less time" and "doubles/halves the speed/throughput/time/latency".

Rule 7 rejects source line-number citations (File.swift:NNN, File.md:NNN, File.py:NNN and a backticked `:NNN`) in Benchmarks/**/*.swift, Sources/VectorCoreBenchmarking/*.swift, README.md, CHANGELOG.md (T13 RD8) and the 13 maintained documents under Docs/, and in the comments (not the string literals) of Tests/**/*.swift (commentOnlyPaths). Other paths, including library sources, are not covered.

Rule 8 (qualitative performance and robustness labels, T13 RD1) covers Sources/**/*.swift, README.md and the 13 maintained documents. It matches only the label list in its pattern (fixture table: fixtures.fail): "optimized" alone (a type-family name), "deterministic", "accurate", "scalable" and "accelerated" are not matched; "fast path(s)" and "fast route(s)" are allowed as branch names (the lookahead also lets "faster/fastest path/route" pass), a hyphenated "fast-path" is matched. The noun forms "efficiency", "robustness" and "reliability" are not matched (live, in non-region sources: the CPUContext chunk-size comment "cache efficiency", Dimension "Balances memory efficiency with expressiveness", the QuantizedKernels "Robustness Check" heading), and an inline hardware claim such as the AlignedMemory comment "Apple Silicon prefers 64-byte alignment (cache line size)" is outside the vocabulary; both are routed (V04-R-0011, V04-R-0012). Its hedge is sentence-scoped like rule 6 and also accepts "no ... guarantee(s)" (the noun, within one clause), "no speed claim" and "not a performance/speed claim"; the check does not verify that the hedge qualifies the label. One exemption (D02 runtime text, Q11).

Rule 9 (rule 6S, T13 RD4) applies rule 6 to Sources/**/*.swift with a multiplier counted only when a speed word is attached ("N x faster/slower/speedup/improvement/throughput/performance/gain", "fastest ... (5-10x)"), so "4x4 tile", "2x unrolling" and a bare "4x" pass; times in ns/µs, ~N ms, percentage speedups or overheads and the spelled-out forms fail unless the sentence is hedged.

Rule 10 (T13 RD5) forbids the spelling zero[- ]?copy in Sources/**/*.swift, README.md and the maintained documents, without a hedge escape; the "-ing" form is matched; other spellings are not seen. Because it is a forbidden phrase, an identifier-shaped "zero-copy" literal is a statement (never excluded).

Vocabulary additions (T13 RD2): "copy-free", "without copying", "no copy/copies"; "handle(s/d/ing) (all) edge cases", "edge-case handling"; "reliable/reliably/reliability", "production-ready/grade/quality", "battle-tested", "bulletproof"; "twice/thrice as|the", "half as fast|the time ...", "N-fold"/"threefold", "order(s) of magnitude". "blazing" was not added (ruling RD2).

Section regions (sectionRegions, T13 RD6): R6 counts only statements whose symbol is a listed section or lies below it; an entry outside the sections and a listed section missing from the file are R8 problems; tombstones apply to the whole file. A statement moved between headings inside the section stays in scope. Today: CHANGELOG.md [Unreleased].

Contracts (T13 RD10): every non-null acceptedContract, split on "/", must be a contracts key; every contract needs a description and a source and must be named by an entry. The source is reviewed text and is not opened or hashed.

Release notes in the CHANGELOG [Unreleased] region that came from an accepted stabilization task cite its closure record as reviewed text (adjacent-invariant), not as an R4 dated artifact, because the unittest harness copies only Sources, Tests, Benchmarks and the ledger's literal paths.

Sentence boundaries (rules 6, 8, 9 and the R5 sentence split) are `.`, `!` or `?` followed by up to two closing characters from `*_)]"'’”` and then whitespace, so "**Not verified.** X is fast." and "(Not verified.) X is fast." are two sentences. Matching text folds the Unicode hyphens U+2010, U+2011, U+2012, U+2013, U+2212 and the soft hyphen U+00AD to "-" (so a non-ASCII hyphen does not evade a hyphenated alternation or the tier-A vocabulary); other look-alikes (U+FE63, U+FF0D) are not folded.
normalization: comment-text-v1: strip ///, //, /* */ and leading *; string literal content with interpolations as \(); NFC; collapse whitespace; lowercase; statement = one doc paragraph or bullet (wrapped lines joined; each line inside a ``` fence separate; `+`-joined single-line literals are one statement); fingerprint = first 16 hex of sha256; Markdown (markdown-text-v1): a .md region or literal forbidden-phrase path is read as prose, one statement per paragraph, list item, table row, heading or fenced-code line, blockquote markers stripped, symbol = heading chain (`section <heading>` joined by ::)

entries.statement: mark: - cache-tiling threshold (issue 1.2)

the 4-way kernels read each candidate's data once, but they iterate lanes innermost, producing `l` (= 128…384) interleaved, strided column streams. above this threshold the tiled kernels are used instead; they read each lane's column as a single sequential stream.

evidence.reference: 4-way loops are lane-inner; tiled kernels are lane-outer

history.originalStatement: the 4-way kernels achieve optimal memory *traffic* (each candidate read once, full cache-line utilization), but they iterate lanes innermost, producing `l` (= 128…384) interleaved, widely-strided column streams. once the candidate buffer exceeds l2, the hardware prefetcher can no longer track `l` streams and demand-miss latency is exposed. above this threshold we switch to the tiled kernels, which read each lane's column as a single sequential stream.

entries.statement: rationale (heuristic; unverified hardware assumption, no crossover is measured in this repository): once the candidate buffer exceeds an l2-sized working budget, the hardware prefetcher may not track `l` streams and demand-miss latency is exposed.

entries.statement: single-position sensitivity (derivable here in one step): $p$ is odd, hence invertible mod $2^{64}$, so $h \mapsto (h \oplus w)\cdot p$ is a bijection of uint64 for every fixed $w$, and for a fixed $h$, $w \mapsto (h \oplus w)\cdot p$ is injective on 32-bit $w$. changing the bit pattern of exactly one element therefore changes that step's output, and every later step is a bijection of the running value, so the final value changes. tests: `benchmarkoutputfoldcontracttests` (`testmatrixconsumerseeseverypositionatallwidthssmalln`, `testfoldsensitivitytosignedzeronanpayloadandorder`).

entries.statement: `clock.now()` is `clock_gettime_nsec_np(clock_uptime_raw)` on macos, ios, tvos and watchos. its tick is `mach_timebase_info.numer / denom` ns rounded up to a whole nanosecond (`ticks`); `testtickformulawithinjectedtimebasevalues` pins the formula with injected values and checks that the running host's tick equals it.

that clock_uptime_raw readings are mach absolute time converted to nanoseconds, so that consecutive readings differ by multiples of that tick, and that the apple silicon timebase is 125/3 (about 41.7 ns) are cited platform facts, not verified by a test here.

on the other platforms `clock.now()` reads `cfabsolutetimegetcurrent()`, returned as `uint64(t * 1e9)`: double seconds since 2001 are quantized to their ulp (about 8.1e8 s gives 2^-23 s, about 119 ns), and the nanosecond product is quantized a second time to its own ulp (128 ns at 8.1e17, 512 ns at 3e18). there the tick is `max(timebase tick, ceil(ulp of the seconds in ns), ceil(ulp of seconds x 1e9))`, cited and derived rather than measured, computed once at startup (`absolutetimetick`; values pinned by `testabsolutetimetickfromthedoubleulp`); that branch is compiled only off macos/ios/tvos/watchos and is unexercised on the hosts this repository tests, while the formula is covered by the pure-function test on every platform.

evidence.limitations: The non-Darwin branch is not compiled on the tested hosts.

entries.statement: when `mach_timebase_info` fails, or off darwin, a conservative 1000 ns (`fallbacknanoseconds`) is used and `source` says so. this is the cited source; it is not a probe of the running host.

evidence.reference: fallbackNanoseconds = 1_000 and the `resolved` fallback branch return it with a "fallback" source string
evidence.limitations: "conservative" is a choice, not a measured bound.

entries.statement: tick of a clock that reports `cfabsolutetime` (double seconds) as `uint64(seconds * 1e9)`: the coarser of two double ulp grids, each rounded up to whole nanoseconds: the ulp of `seconds` (converted to ns) and the ulp of the product `seconds * 1e9`. never below `timebasetick`; a non-finite or implausibly large (>= 1e18 ns) grid gives `max(timebasetick, fallbacknanoseconds)`. pure and platform independent so it can be tested with injected epochs (`testabsolutetimetickfromthedoubleulp`).

evidence.domain: injected epochs incl. 0, negative, NaN, inf, 1e300
evidence.limitations: Pure function; platform clock not exercised.

entries.statement: two quantization grids: the double seconds themselves, and the product `uint64(seconds * 1e9)` that `clock.now()` returns, which is rounded a second time to the ulp of the nanosecond-scale double. the smallest nonzero difference between two readings is the coarser of the two (and never finer than the timebase tick). values pinned by `testabsolutetimetickfromthedoubleulp`.

evidence.limitations: Pinned values, not a proof for every epoch.

entries.statement: # vectorcore performance guide

this guide covers choosing vector types, provider and batch configuration, matrix routing, memory use, and measuring vectorcore with the `vectorcore-bench` executable. it makes no speed claim beyond the dated one-host record in [measured workload envelope (one host)](#measured-workload-envelope-one-host), which cites `benchmarks/workloadenvelope/results.md`: every other statement below about speed is marked as not verified in this repository, and the stored baselines in `benchmarks/baselines/` are historical, machine-specific records. measure on your own hardware and workload (see [benchmarking](#benchmarking)).

evidence.limitations: Speed is not measured by any test or dated artifact in this repository. L04 carves out the dated one-host record Benchmarks/WorkloadEnvelope/RESULTS.md, cited from the Measured Workload Envelope section.

entries.statement: the gemm result agrees with the per-pair kernels to **~1e-3 relative**, **not bit-identical**. the difference comes from evaluating distance through the `‖x‖² + ‖y‖² − 2⟨x, y⟩` identity (rather than summing `(xᵢ − yᵢ)²` directly) plus the final clamp: euclidean is **squared** and clamped `≥ 0` (the identity can round slightly negative when `x ≈ y`); cosine is `1 − cos` clamped to `[0, 2]`. if you need exact per-pair values, set `enablematrixrouting = false`.

entries.statement: **correctness gate.** a report records a correctness failure, which the comparison above rejects with exit 2, when a case's comparison with its double reference exceeds the case's threshold. the euclidean and squared-euclidean `batch` routes, their `boundary` companions and the `matrix` routes are held to thresholds derived from each route's worst-case rounding bound for the case's dimension and candidate count: `γ_k = k·u/(1 − k·u)` with `u = 2^-24` and `k` counted from the route's summation (`correctnesspolicy` in `benchmarks/vectorcorebench/utils/correctnesspolicy.swift`; `testderivedthresholdsfollowtheroundingcounts` and `testgenericsquaredeuclideanboundholdsandstillcatchesdroppedwork` in `benchmarkcorrectnesspolicytests`). the `matrix` routes are gated on absolute error, because their diagonal references are zero (`testmatrixzeroreferenceisgatedonabsoluteerror`), and a relative error never divides by a reference smaller than 1 (`testrelativeerrorneverdividesbyreferencebelowfloor`). the bounds for the `batch.euclidean` `generic` routes (`vdsp_distancesq`) and the `matrix` routes (`vdsp_svesq`, `cblas_sgemm`) assume that accelerate evaluates each inner product with binary32 operations in some order, not with a fast matrix-multiplication algorithm; that assumption is not verified. the thresholds are worst-case bounds, so a defect that moves a result by less than its threshold, such as one small term dropped from one distance, passes them. the other validated routes keep fixed relative thresholds (fp32 `1e-6`, fp16 `2e-3`, fp16 cosine `3e-3`), which are not derived from their summations and are not verified to bound their rounding error.

evidence.domain: CorrectnessPolicy rules for every case ID of the Euclidean and squared-Euclidean batch routes, their boundary companions and the matrix routes at D in {512, 768, 1536}; actual route outputs on the run-seed-0 fixtures at the CI recipe sizes (N 100 and 1000; matrix N 1, 3, 8, 17)
evidence.limitations: The thresholds are worst-case bounds under the standard rounding model; the Accelerate routes (vDSP_distancesq, vDSP_svesq, cblas_sgemm) rest on the stated assumption that they are binary32 inner products in some order, marked not verified in the statement. The pass-through sentence follows from the thresholds by definition. The fixed thresholds of the other routes are stated as not verified.

entries.statement: domain: ‖q‖² · ‖c‖² < float.greatestfinitemagnitude, narrower than the documented cosine domain ‖v‖² < float.greatestfinitemagnitude (docs/numerical_behavior.md). the denominator is sqrt(‖q‖² · ‖c‖²), so when that product overflows the call takes the end branch and returns 1 for finite inputs in any direction, parallel ones included (adjacent code; not in the t15 table). fp16 × fp16 (`cosinefp16core`) cannot reach this at widths up to 1536: each finite squared norm is at most 1536 · 65504² up to float rounding, so their product stays far below float.greatestfinitemagnitude.

evidence.reference: let magnitude = sqrt(qMagSq * cMagSq); the clamped branch needs magnitude > 1e-9 && magnitude.isFinite, otherwise guard qMagSq.isFinite && cMagSq.isFinite else { return .nan }; return 1.0. A finite FP16 value is at most 65504 in magnitude, so a 1536-wide FP16 squared norm is at most 1536 * 65504^2 (about 6.6e12) and a product of two such norms is about 4.3e25 at most
evidence.domain: cosineMixedCore (FP32 x FP16, either order) and, for the last sentence, cosineFP16Core at widths 512, 768 and 1536
evidence.limitations: Not exercised by a test: no T15 fixture has two finite squared norms whose product overflows. The FP16 bound ignores Float rounding of the accumulated sums, which is far below the margin.

entries.statement: ## api and performance

allocation behavior depends on the type and operation. generic [`dimensionstorage`](sources/vectorcore/storage/dimensionstorage.swift) defaults to managed heap storage above 16 elements. results, copies, and batch scratch storage may allocate. there is no package-wide allocation-free guarantee.

evidence.limitations: The remaining sentences are disclaimers ("may allocate", "no package-wide allocation-free guarantee").

entries.statement: measure performance in release on your workload. the [top-k benchmark record](benchmarks/topknancontract/results.md) gives a specific before/after comparison with hardware, samples, and limitations; it does not measure allocations or establish a universal speedup. see [contribution benchmark instructions](contributing.md#performance-changes).

evidence.domain: the Top-K before/after record it links
evidence.limitations: The record is one host; the statement says it does not measure allocations or establish a universal speedup.

entries.symbol: section VectorCore::section Numerical behavior and unsafe buffers
entries.statement: floating-point operations can overflow, propagate non-finite values, and produce slightly different results across kernels. validation and error behavior are api-specific: check the selected api's contract when handling zero norms, nans, infinities, or untrusted dimensions. a throwing initializer or checked operation does not imply that every subsequent operation validates its inputs.
entries.reason: General caution that points readers to each API contract; it asserts no property of a specific API.

entries.symbol: section VectorCore::section Numerical behavior and unsafe buffers
entries.statement: `topkselection` orders numeric scores, including infinities, before nans. its default tie policy prefers smaller original indices; exact ties include signed zeros and pairs of nans. for positive `k`, selection retains nans when needed to return `min(k, count)` candidates. these contracts are exercised by [topknancontracttests](tests/comprehensivetests/topknancontracttests.swift). metric computation can round differently before selection; this ordering rule does not promise identical results for different computed scores. see [numerical behavior](docs/numerical_behavior.md) for score conventions, matrix precision tradeoffs, and api-specific non-finite handling.

evidence.reference: TopKSelection doc "Selection contract" and `TopKSelection.orderedBefore`; the README names the TopKNaNContractTests suite (e.g. numericInfinityOutranksNaN, exactTiesAndSignedZeroKeepOriginalPositionsAndBits, nanCandidatesFillRemainingPositions)
evidence.limitations: The README cites the suite, not methods, so R3 cannot resolve it; the methods above were checked by name.

entries.symbol: section VectorCore::section Numerical behavior and unsafe buffers
entries.statement: for unsafe apis, callers must provide valid counts, initialized elements, required alignment, and sufficient storage; respect aliasing and exclusivity rules. pointers borrowed by a closure must not escape that closure. keep owned allocations alive until all consumers finish, and coordinate mutation and ownership transfer across tasks. see [memory alignment](docs/memory_alignment.md) and [unifiedvectorbuffer](sources/vectorcore/storage/unifiedvectorbuffer.swift).
entries.reason: Caller obligations for unsafe APIs; no property of the library is asserted.

entries.symbol: section VectorCore::section Numerical behavior and unsafe buffers
entries.statement: the package enables swift 6 strict concurrency checking, but some buffer and pool types use `@unchecked sendable`, which relies on manually maintained invariants. `memorypool` is a class with explicit synchronization. neither conformance nor compiler checking makes arbitrary shared pointer mutation safe.

evidence.reference: Package.swift targets pass `.enableExperimentalFeature("StrictConcurrency")`; MemoryPool holds `private let stateLock = NSLock()`; several buffer types declare `@unchecked Sendable`
evidence.limitations: The last sentence is a disclaimer.

entries.statement: vectorcore contains cpu implementations and buffer/provider interfaces for integration with the separate vectoraccelerate package. `unifiedvectorbuffer` provides a scoped contiguous read view; it does **not** imply page alignment. `pagealignedbuffer` and opt-in page-aligned soa storage provide additional allocation contracts. gpu import, ownership, and synchronization require the consumer to follow those contracts. see [package boundaries](docs/package_boundaries.md) and [soa layout contract](docs/soa_layout_contract.md).

evidence.reference: UnifiedVectorBuffer.swift: the optimized types report `MemoryLayout<SIMD4<Float>>.alignment` and DynamicVector `MemoryLayout<Float>.alignment`; only PageAlignedBuffer reports the page size
evidence.limitations: Page alignment of PageAlignedBuffer is pinned by UnifiedVectorBufferTests.pageAlignmentContract.

entries.statement: deployment targets are distinct from tested configurations. the [september 6 verification record](docs/verification-topk-nan-contract-2026-09-05.md) records full debug and release tests on apple m3 max, macos 26.5.2, swift 6.3.3. the [ci workflow](.github/workflows/ci.yml) defines the current macos test and apple platform compile matrix; consult its run results for coverage on a given commit. simulator compilation does not establish runtime behavior on devices. linux is not a supported or tested platform for this package.

evidence.reference: Docs/verification-topk-nan-contract-2026-09-05.md records the September 6 full Debug and Release runs on Apple M3 Max, macOS 26.5.2, Swift 6.3.3
evidence.limitations: One host; cited as reviewed text (the harness copy omits Docs records); the CI and platform sentences are policy and pointers, not measurements.

entries.statement: vectorcore is pre-1.0. minor releases may change apis or numerical behavior; patch releases aim to preserve source compatibility but may correct documented bugs. read release notes and test updates against your workload. see [contributing](contributing.md#compatibility-and-support) for support policy.

entries.statement: the optimized types and `dynamicvector` conform to `unifiedvectorbuffer`. the four optimized types also conform to `soacompatible`; `dynamicvector` does not. these conformances are separate from `vectorprotocol` and do not imply that every type participates in every optimized route.

entries.symbol: section VectorCore API overview::section Search and matrix routing
entries.statement: `matrixdistance` materializes the query-by-candidate score matrix, and the pairwise matrix route returns the full n × n matrix, computed one query row at a time straight into the returned rows with no separate score buffer; the `.gram` route of `findnearestbatch` scores one query tile against one candidate tile at a time. an `into:` output or prepared candidates can reuse particular storage, but does not make the operation allocation-free. callers of `matrixdistance` must validate every input dimension and provide representable sizes and correctly sized output buffers; it is not a checked replacement for the throwing search entry points. see [numerical behavior](numerical_behavior.md).

entries.statement: - **breaking: `searchresult.computedscore` is replaced by `computedscore(using:)`, and search results now carry relevance scores.** `distancemetric` gains a defaulted `relevancescore(for:)` requirement (default `nil`). the six inverse-distance builtins score finite nonnegative distances as `1 / (1 + d)`; `dotproductdistance` uses the logistic `1 / (1 + exp(d))`. producer results from `simplevectorcollection` and the default `vectorcollection.search` now populate `score` for the selected results. migration: use `.score`, or call `.computedscore(using: metric)` with the metric that produced the distance. because `searchresult` has synthesized `equatable` over `score`, `producerresult == searchresult(id:, distance:)` is now false for builtin metrics; `hashable` still hashes only `id` and `distance`.

entries.statement: - **breaking: `vectormath.nearestneighbors(query:in:k:using:)` now follows the shared top-k selection policy.** results are ordered by ascending numeric distance, nan distances come after every numeric one, and exact ties (including `+0`/`-0` and two nans) keep the smaller original index, as in `topkselection.select(k:from:)`. before, a plain `<` sort left nan positions unspecified (distances `[nan, 1, 0]` with `k = 3` returned indices `[0, 2, 1]`; now `[2, 1, 0]`). `k <= 0` and an empty candidate array now return `[]` without calling the metric; before, `k == 0` called it once per candidate and a negative `k` trapped after calling it once per candidate. for positive `k` the metric still runs exactly once per candidate in index order and the result still has `min(k, vectors.count)` entries. selection keeps a bounded heap of `min(k, n)` entries when `min(k, n) < n / 10` and sorts all `n` pairs otherwise. migration: callers that depended on nan positions or on the negative-`k` trap must handle the new order and the empty result.

entries.statement: - **breaking: generic small-`k` `operations.findnearest` streams each candidate through `parallelreduce`, without autotuning calibration.** this route applies when no `batchkernelprovider` is installed, `min(k, n) < n / 10` and no optimized route does: any metric on `dynamicvector`, `vector<d>` or `vector384optimized`; any metric except euclidean, cosine and dot product on `vector512optimized`; and any metric except euclidean and cosine on `vector768optimized` and `vector1536optimized`. before, the first search for a cold autotuning (dimension, kernel) key evaluated up to 256 candidates twice (calibration probes, then scoring) and published a tuning, unless autotuning was disabled (`vc_autotune=0`), its calibration-time budget was spent or that key was being calibrated at the same moment; and a candidate count below the tuned break-even used a synchronous map that never called the installed `computeprovider` (observed on the unchanged base: 200 metric calls for 100 candidates, no provider call). now, on a successful return, the metric has run exactly once per candidate, in index order within each range the provider supplies to one `parallelreduce` call (the overload without a chunk hint), each range keeping a heap of at most `min(k, range count)` entries; this route calibrates and publishes no tuning. the provider's own serial, bounded and nested policies decide the partition, call order across ranges is unspecified, and a cancelled task now gets `cancellationerror` from this route before its next metric call (the provider checks around each callback and the scan checks before each metric call); before, a run below the tuned break-even completed without checking (observed on the unchanged base with 64 candidates). large `k`, the 512/768/1536 optimized euclidean routes, cosine and dot on `vector512optimized`, and cosine on `vector768optimized` and `vector1536optimized` (which still scores every candidate with the fused kernels, after any calibration) keep their routes and their cancellation behaviour: below the tuned break-even a cancelled large-`k` or cosine 768/1536 search can still return a complete result. `findnearestbatch`'s per-query fallback now validates the candidate rows once per batch instead of once per query. migration: metrics with side effects see `n` calls per successful search instead of up to `n + 256`; a custom `computeprovider` now receives `parallelreduce` for these searches and must honour its range and combine contract; do not rely on a small-`k` search to warm an autotuning key.

entries.statement: - **optimized-vector hashing now covers every coordinate.** `hash(into:)` on `vector384optimized`, `vector512optimized`, `vector768optimized` and `vector1536optimized` feeds every simd4 storage block in order, then the dimension. before, it fed only the first two and last two blocks plus the dimension, so vectors that differed only in the other coordinates always hashed equally and collided in a `set` or `dictionary`. equality and storage are unchanged, and float `hashable` semantics apply, so `+0` and `-0` still hash equally. each hash is now o(d) in the dimension and is not cached. hash values remain process-seeded by swift's `hasher`: they can differ between processes and must not be persisted, and collisions remain legal. covered by `optimizedhashcontracttests` and `scripts/ci/tests/test_optimized_hash_coverage.py`. a single-host record, not a performance claim (release, swift 6.4, mac15,9; medians of 1,024-hash invocations, before and after measured in one session): per hash, 44.9 → 744.3 ns at 384 (16.6×), 45.4 → 949.8 ns at 512 (20.9×), 48.1 → 1,451.0 ns at 768 (30.2×) and 45.2 → 2,880.5 ns at 1536 (63.7×). on the same host, `dictionary` insert-plus-lookup over corpora that differ only in interior coordinates took longer at 64 vectors and less time at 512 and 1,024 vectors, at every width.

entries.statement: - **arm64 batch fp16 encoding canonicalizes nan.** on arm64, `mixedprecisionkernels.platformoptimizedconvertbatch` now encodes every nan in its simd4 chunks to the quiet nan `sign | 0x7e00`, consistent with the scalar converter and the batch tail. chunk lanes used to keep the high payload bits, so one buffer could mix nan encodings. for example, the fp32 nan `0x7fc12345` now encodes to `0x7e00` (it was `0x7e09`), and `0xffffe000` to `0xfe00` (it was `0xffff`). non-nan results are unchanged: all 2^32 fp32 inputs were compared before and after on one arm64 host (records outside this repository). decoding still maps every fp16 nan to `0x7fc00000`, and no other conversion path changed. the policy is pinned for the scalar, simd8, batch, vector, soa and `platformoptimizedconvertbatch` conversion paths by [fp16converterexhaustivetests](tests/comprehensivetests/fp16converterexhaustivetests.swift), which also checks all 65,536 decodes, all 63,490 non-nan round trips and 190,464 rounding midpoints and neighbours against integer references.

entries.statement: - **breaking: cosine distance no longer turns nan or infinite inputs into a perfect match.** every cosine distance path (`cosinedistance` and its `vector{512,768,1536}optimized` overloads, the `batchkernels` fused and pre-normalized range kernels, the `batchkernels_soa` cosine kernels, the fp16 and mixed-precision cosine kernels, `vectorprotocol.cosinedistance(to:)` and `distance(to:metric: .cosine)`, and the `operations`, `batchoperations`, `topkselection`, `vectormath` and `vectorcollection` searches built on them) now returns nan when either vector has a nan or infinite coordinate, including against a zero vector. previously `min(1, nan)` mapped a nan similarity to distance 0, so such rows ranked nearest on the fused routes (and ±∞ rows on the generic routes); the `[-1, 1]` clamp now applies only to finite similarities, so the top-k rule ranks these rows after every numeric distance. apart from the finite changes listed in this entry, finite results were bit-identical in the t15 phase 2 probe comparison (1,954 finite rows against the phase 1 baseline run; one host; records outside this repository: `t15/phase2/runs/phase2-compare.txt` and `t15/phase1/runs/attempt3-testable/run.stdout` in the stabilization records; not pinned by a test). `cosinesimilarity` on `vectorprotocol`, the optimized vectors and the array simd providers returns nan for a non-finite magnitude (was 0), and the optimized vectors and array providers return 0 instead of nan when two tiny nonzero magnitudes multiply to zero; `[vector<dim768>].cosinesimilaritymatrix()` returns nan where it passed a non-finite score through. `vectorprotocol.cosinedistance(to:)` now clamps finite rounding overshoot to [0, 2] (it could return a small negative distance). two zero vectors now have cosine distance 1 on every path (the fused kernels and the fp16 single-pair kernels returned 0). each path keeps its own zero-vector threshold, unchanged, and the new value applies to whatever that path already treats as zero: on the fused kernels this includes vectors whose squared norms are at or below `float.leastnormalmagnitude`. vectors whose squared norm overflows float (`‖v‖² ≥ float.greatestfinitemagnitude`) are outside the supported domain: the per-pair paths can return nan (two such parallel vectors returned 0) or 1 where `matrixdistance` returns the true distance, and the array simd providers' `cosinesimilarity`, whose float sum of squares overflows there, returns nan (was 0). the mixed-precision cosine kernels that pair an fp32 vector with an fp16 vector have a narrower domain: the product of the two squared norms must stay below `float.greatestfinitemagnitude`; past it they return 1 for finite inputs in any direction, as before. migration: filter or validate non-finite embeddings before search if nan distances are unwanted; code that relied on 0 or 1 for such rows must test `isnan`. pinned by [t15cosineexceptionaltabletests](tests/comprehensivetests/t15cosineexceptionaltabletests.swift) (every registered implementation) and [t15cosineselectiontests](tests/comprehensivetests/t15cosineselectiontests.swift) (every public cosine search route). `scripts/ci/tests/test_cosine_registry.py` is a lexical guard that keeps the registry complete: it fails when a body it discovers (a name containing "cosine", a clamp idiom, a call of the shared helper, or a body in a cosine-named type) is unregistered or a registry entry is stale. its clamp rule is a body-level token check (an `isfinite` or `isnan` token in the same body), not proof that the clamp is guarded; the table is the semantic check.

entries.statement: - **fp16 portability on intel macos and mac catalyst.** remove unconditional uses of native `float16`, which these intel sdk targets mark unavailable. the 512/768/1536 fp16 buffers retain portable `uint16` storage and classify finite values from their exponent bits. native conversion remains opt-in; `detectoverflow(value:)`, whose return type is `float16?`, is excluded on those intel targets. use `canrepresent(_:)` or `validatebatch(values:)` for fp32 range checks there. regression coverage: [mixedprecisionrangevalidationtests](tests/comprehensivetests/mixedprecisionrangevalidationtests.swift).

entries.statement: - **fp16 kernels no longer heap-allocate on each 8-lane load.** a module-internal `unsaferawpointer.loadunaligned(as:)` extension shadowed the standard library's allocation-free `loadunaligned` inside vectorcore. each `simd8<uint16>` load in the fp16 range kernels (`range_{euclid2,cosine,dot}_mixed_*`), pair kernels (`dotfp16_*`, `dotmixed*`, `euclidean*`, `cosine*`), batch kernels (`batchdotfp16_*`, `batchdotmixed*`) and `tofp32()` allocated, copied and freed 16 bytes. the extension is removed, together with an unused `unsaferawbufferpointer` companion. the binary serialization reads already used the standard-library overload, and their allocation counts are unchanged (t12 emitted-code inspection and allocation probe, one host; records outside this repository). kernel outputs are unchanged: t12's fixture probe found them byte-identical before and after (one host, records outside this repository). one-host release measurement (arm64, macos 27.0.1), allocation events per call over 4,096 candidates: `range_euclid2_mixed_512` fell from 262,145 to 1 (by size, inferred to be the per-call candidate-handle array), `range_euclid2_mixed_1536` from 786,433 to 1 and `batchdotfp16_512` from 524,289 to 1. single-pair calls such as `dotfp16_512` fell from 128 to 0. `scripts/ci/tests/test_no_stdlib_member_shadows.py` now rejects module extensions that redeclare curated standard-library raw-pointer or simd members, except two pinned `simd.sum()` declarations, allowlisted pending a routed semantic review (t14).

entries.statement: `.gram` rows: each holds `min(k, vectors.count)` entries in ascending score order, computed nans after numeric scores and exact score ties by the smaller original index. euclidean membership and order use the squared scores, then each squared score `s` returns `s` if it is nan, its square root if it is positive and 0 otherwise, so two entries whose roots are equal keep the order of their squared scores (`p02gramroutetests.selectionmatchessortedtilescores`). the result always holds `queries.count` rows of `min(k, vectors.count)` entries, outside the payload limit: `k >= vectors.count` returns every candidate for every query. gram scores are a different arithmetic from `findnearest`; see `batchsearchcpustrategy.gram` for the derived error bound and what it does not promise.

evidence.domain: three widths, both metrics, near/rand/offset1000/exceptional fixtures, five tile geometries, k = 10 and Int.max; root ties: P02GramRouteTests.equalRootsKeepSquaredOrder
evidence.limitations: Membership is checked against the scores the route itself emitted; their accuracy is P02GramAccuracyTests.

entries.statement: - `.gram`: `task.checkcancellation()` runs after the plan and limit succeed and before any scratch or result allocation, at each query-tile and candidate-tile boundary, after each tile's scores are computed, before each result row is allocated and filled, and before the result is returned; a cancelled search throws `cancellationerror` without a partial result (`p02gramcancellationtests.precancelledvalidplandoesnowork`, `p02gramcancellationtests.cancellationateveryeventstopsatthenextcheckpoint`). packing, normalization, a blas call or the fill of one row is not interrupted once started, so the work between two checks depends on the tile rows and `k`; there is no latency or memory-release deadline. a cancellation that arrives after the last check does not affect the returned result.

evidence.domain: Vector512Optimized, both metrics, three tile geometries, cancellation at every traced event

entries.statement: - **breaking: `operations.findnearestbatch` no longer switches to a gemm route by itself.** before, without a `batchkernelprovider`, at least 8 queries and 256 candidates with euclidean or cosine distance on a 512, 768 or 1536 optimized type took a gemm route, a different arithmetic that `enablematrixrouting` did not affect: on the offset-1000 rows, on one test host (apple silicon, accelerate), it returned a candidate at distance 0.0 whose true distance is 0.125, recorded as the failure of `p02defaultrouteredtests.offset1000analyticoracle` before this change (the test now pins the new default). now the default, `cpustrategy: .perquery`, runs `findnearest`'s routes for every query at every batch size, so each row has the indices and score bits that `findnearest` returns for its query (`p02defaultrouteredtests.defaultrouteequalssinglequery`). for the inputs that took the gemm route this changes scores and rankings, and the work and temporary storage: no queries × candidates score matrix is built, and each query runs its own single-query search. on one test host (p02 phase g allocation probe, not a test) the old route requested a buffer of q × n floats on every call at q 8 with n 256 and at q 64 with n 4096, and the new default requested none that large. the new default is slower in most measured cases: on that host (two one-host timing records, medians of 9 samples, not tests: the p02 phase g record of 2026-10-07, on a quiet machine, and a high-power re-run of 2026-10-16 with two repetitions, both outside this repository) every measured case at q 64 with n 4096 took longer, for example about 57 ms instead of about 2.4 to 2.5 ms per call for euclidean distance at 1536, about 23 times as long (22.6-23.9× across the records), and about 21 ms instead of about 1.3 to 1.5 ms at 512, about 14 to 16 times as long (13.7-15.9×); euclidean distance at q 8 with n 256 took about 2.8 to 4.4 times as long (2.75-4.43×); cosine distance at q 8 with n 256, and every measured case at q 7 with n 256, took less time in every record (cosine at 1536 with q 7 by 0.3% in one high-power repetition, effectively equal). to score a large batch with the gemm route, opt in with `cpustrategy: .gram(...)`. the default batch search can now be cancelled through the provider's and `findnearest`'s checks (`p02perqueryroutetests.precancelleddefaultthrowsbeforeanymetriccall`); the gemm route had no cancellation check. the gemm route remains available as `cpustrategy: .gram(...)`. a reference to the function by its full name `findnearestbatch(queries:in:k:metric:)` must add `cpustrategy:`, and the error context captured in debug builds names `findnearestbatch(queries:in:k:metric:cpustrategy:)`.

entries.statement: - **breaking: `isnormalized`, and four norms in code generic over the dimension, bind to `vector`'s own members.** with the constraint gone, `vector.isnormalized` (true when `abs(magnitudesquared - 1) < 1e-6`, computed on every read) is `vector`'s `indexablevector` witness for every dimension, built-in ones included. code generic over `indexablevector` or over the dimension (`func f<d: staticdimension>(_ v: vector<d>)`) read the protocol default `false` before and now reads the check. in code generic over the dimension, `l1norm`, `linfinitynorm`, `manhattandistance(to:)` and `chebyshevdistance(to:)` also bind to `vector`'s members instead of the `vectorprotocol` extension: their results equal the concrete calls' bit for bit, and they read `operations.simdprovider` (`l1norm` and `manhattandistance(to:)` above 32 elements), so an installed provider now applies to them (`genericoverdimensionequalsconcrete`). `dynamicvector`, the `vector*optimized` types and `normalizationhint` are unchanged (`indexableisnormalizedwitness`).

evidence.domain: Vector<Dim4>, Vector<Dim512>, DynamicVector, Vector512Optimized and NormalizationHint in generic and existential calls; generic-over-D against concrete reads of the five members on Dim2, Dim128 and Dim512, also under a recording provider
evidence.limitations: The before-state (protocol default false; VectorProtocol-extension norms for generic-over-D code) is derived from Swift overload and witness rules, the base symbol graph and reviewer A2's minimal-package model, not run by a test at the base.

entries.statement: - **vectorcorec: `vc_dot_int8` has a defined result for every input.** it returns the exact integer dot product reduced modulo 2^32 and read in the int32 range, on the scalar, arm64 sdot, arm64 neon and x86_64 avx2 paths. before, the scalar loop and the final tail additions accumulated in signed `int32_t`, which overflowed (undefined behavior) when a partial sum left the int32 range; block loops now test the remaining count, so the index cannot wrap. the swift package build does not call it (`vc_use_c_kernels` is not defined). covered by `dispatcherfollowsthemodulolaw` and `scripts/ci/tests/d02ccontract.py`; the x86_64 path was cross-compiled, not executed.

entries.statement: - **lapack workspace check on near-square inputs (introduced after `v0.3.3`, fixed before release).** `v0.3.3` is not affected: its shim sized each workspace from accelerate's answer and rejected none. earlier in this release cycle the shim began checking accelerate's workspace answers and treated its reference bounds (4k² + 7k for the svd) as minimums for them. with the default lapack provider, `lapacklinearalgebraprovider.svdthin` and `pcamodel.fit` then threw `.operationfailed` ("sgesdd returned an invalid workspace query") on shapes where lapack's `sgesdd` does not qr-factor first (max(m, n) < ⌊11·min(m, n)/6⌋) and accelerate's answer was below the bound: for example exact pca (`pcaconfig(oversampling: int.max)`) of 500 samples in dimension 384 or 768, and sketch-path fits whose ℓ×d panel has that shape. in t19's sweep that was every such shape with min(m, n) = 64, only max(m, n) ≤ 17 with min(m, n) = 16, and none with min(m, n) = 8. this entry fixes the check before release: the svd, symmetric-eigen and qr bounds are now allocation floors only. the shim allocates the larger of accelerate's answer (plus the existing headroom) and the bound, and still rejects non-finite, non-positive and unrepresentable answers. regression coverage, `t19lapackworkspacequerytests` against designed spectra: `svdthinsweepcrossespathfive` and `exactpcasweepcrossespathfive` (across the boundary, tall and wide), `reportedcellssucceed`, `randomizedpcawidepanelscrosspathfive` (two sketch-path panels), and the near-boundary `symmetriceigennearboundaryshapes` and `qrthinnearboundaryshapes`.

evidence.domain: the default LAPACK provider on Apple platforms: every R in r...2r for r in {8, 16, 64}, tall and wide, default LAPACK provider, designed spectra; the reported 500×384, 500×768 and 1000×1536 cells; two sketch-path panels on path 5t; near-boundary symmetricEigen and qrThin shapes
evidence.limitations: Other shapes and other Accelerate versions are not exercised; the vendor answers are observed, not specified. The v0.3.3 sentence rests on the v0.3.3 tag's Sources/VectorCoreC/common/vc_lapack.c (vc__lwork_from_query: ceil + 1/64 + 1, clamped to INT32_MAX, no rejection) and on no tag containing ed95f95 (T19 review I1), not on a test.

evidence.domain: the one-host grid of Benchmarks/WorkloadEnvelope/RESULTS.md: N 50-100,000, D 384/768/1536, PCA K=50 (49 at N=50), kNN k=15, default 2-D UMAP; synthetic 50-cluster unit-norm data; Apple M3 Max, macOS 27.0.1, Swift 6.4, Release

entries.statement: **not measured.** inputs outside this grid are not measured: n above 100,000, d above 1536, other k, k, epochs or configurations, other linear-algebra providers and other vector types. no size limit applies to them beyond the documented representability checks (lp64 blas dimensions and int element and byte counts, which throw `vectorerror.invaliddimension`; see the `- throws:` lists of these apis and [linear algebra and projection](linear_algebra_and_projection.md)). passing those checks does not promise that allocation succeeds, and their time and memory are not promised. these calls are synchronous and cannot be cancelled.

evidence.limitations: No measurement or test covers them.

entries.statement: - **breaking: fixed-size vector storage must have the type's lane count (s01).** on the optimized fp32 types and the int8 types, a raw, replacement, nested or `inout` storage write with the wrong lane count now traps with a required-count diagnostic in debug and release builds. the public `storage` of `vector384optimized`, `vector512optimized`, `vector768optimized`, `vector1536optimized`, `vector512int8`, `vector768int8` and `vector1536int8` is now a computed property (a guarded setter and a `_modify` that checks the count) over private backing storage: valid source compiles unchanged, but the stored layout changes, so binaries must be rebuilt. the int8 types gain explicit `codable` (`init(from:)`, `encode(to:)`) that throws `decodingerror.datacorrupted` for a malformed storage shape; the keys `storage` and `quantizationparams` and the wire representation are unchanged. `dynamicvector`'s dimension follows its current storage count, so replacing its storage can change its dimension. custom conformers must still report a truthful `scalarcount` and buffer shape; that is not mechanically enforced.

entries.statement: - **breaking: `typedbufferpool` has a byte cap and returns lease handles, and the actor pools own their allocations (e04).** `typedbufferpool.init(maxbufferspersize:)` is removed: use `typedbufferpool(maxcachedbytes:maxbufferspersize:)` (`maxcachedbytes` is required; `maxbufferspersize` still defaults to 10). `acquire(count:)` returns an immutable `typedbufferpool<element>.handle` (`buffer`, `pointer`, `count`) instead of an `unsafemutablebufferpointer<element>`, and `release(_:)` takes that handle; `withbuffer(count:_:)`, `cachedbytes`, `activebytes` and `clear()` are new. `bufferprovider` gains `withbuffer(size:_:)`, an `async throws` helper with a `sendable` body and result that awaits the release on both exits, and `swiftbufferpool` gains `cachedbytes`. an invalid `swiftbufferpool` size throws the new `buffererror.invalidrequest(size:)`, so an exhaustive `switch` over `buffererror` must handle that case. `typedbufferpool` and `swiftbufferpool` own both checked-out and cached allocations: each acquisition is a fresh lease; a return validates identity, count and address; cache admission counts physical payload bytes and never exceeds the byte or per-size cap; clearing releases cached storage while active leases stay valid. generic storage is uninitialized when acquired: initialize and deinitialize exactly the elements you use before returning it. handles are borrowed metadata: keep the pool alive until the release, do not use a pointer after it, and synchronize pointee access yourself. a scoped body keeps its lease until it finishes, even if it ignores cancellation. `memorypool.bufferhandle` now retains an allocation owner and a weak pool, and its `count` is stored instead of computed, so binaries must be rebuilt; memorypool handles may outlive their pool, an invalid memorypool acquisition returns `nil`, and a nonpositive, nonfinite or beyond-horizon timer interval disables automatic cleanup.

entries.statement: - **Release builds check the output capacity of the FP16 SoA batch kernels and the row shapes of `MatrixDistance`.** The fifteen public `MixedPrecisionKernels.batchEuclidean{512,768,1536}`, `batchDotProductSoA` and `batchEuclideanBlocked{512,768,1536}` SoA kernels, the six public `batchDotFP16_{512,768,1536}` and `batchDotMixed{512,768,1536}` array kernels (through two shared internal kernels) and the nine internal SoA kernels behind the optimized batch routes checked the output count only under `#if DEBUG`, so a Release caller passing a buffer shorter than the candidate count was written past its end with no diagnostic. They now stop with a named `fatalError` before any write, in every build; the mixed-precision range core's own capacity and range preconditions are active in every build as well. The policy test `test_release_active_capacity_guards.py` fails on any new Debug-only capacity assert in `Sources/VectorCore`. `MatrixDistance.prepare` and the six matrix entries took the dimension from the first row and copied that many bytes from every row, reading past a shorter row; every packed row must now have that dimension, checked by a named `fatalError` in every build. `ReleaseSizeGuardTests.kernelTrapsBeforeWriting` and `matrixRowsOfUnequalLengthTrap` run each case in a child process on the Debug and Release rows and check that the output it was given is untouched.

evidence.domain: FP16 SoA kernel output capacity; MatrixDistance row shape
evidence.limitations: One undersized-buffer shape (4 slots for 8 candidates) and one short-row shape per entry; the guard is a count comparison, so other shapes follow from the same branch.

entries.statement: - **Pool teardown leaks active leases instead of freeing them, and the `MemoryPool` cleanup timer no longer depends on the width of `Int`.** Destroying a `TypedBufferPool`, a `SwiftBufferPool` or the internal `BufferPool` while a lease was still checked out freed that lease, so a `Handle` or `BufferHandle` that outlived its pool pointed at freed memory and the first write through it was a silent use-after-free. The three pools now leak active leases on teardown and still free their cached allocations, as 0.3.3 did, so an escaped handle stays valid (`BufferPoolOwnershipTests.internalAndTypedDestructionOwnCachedAndLeakActive`, `swiftPoolDestructionLeaksActiveLease`); the lease contract is unchanged: release every handle before dropping the pool. `MemoryPool` compared the cleanup interval against `Double(Int.max) / 1e9`, which is 2.147 s on a 32-bit `Int` (arm64_32 watchOS devices, inside the declared floor), so the default 30 s interval silently disabled automatic cleanup there; the bound is now the 64-bit nanosecond horizon on every platform (`MemoryPoolBoundaryTests.timerHorizonIsIndependentOfIntWidth`).

evidence.domain: pool teardown with active leases; MemoryPool cleanup-timer horizon
evidence.limitations: The arm64_32 figure (2.147 s) is arithmetic on the former guard, not a measurement on a device; no CI leg builds arm64_32.

entries.statement: - **`ComputeProvider`'s chunk-hinted defaults call the hint-less requirements.** The default `parallelForEach(items:minChunk:)` and `parallelReduce(items:initial:minChunk:_:_:)` validate `minChunk` and then call the hint-less requirement, the direction 0.3.3 used, so a conformer that implements only the hint-less overloads (the ones the 0.3.3 guide named) is reached by every optimized search route and its `maxConcurrency` is not consulted by those defaults. During development the direction had been reversed, which bypassed such conformers and threw `invalidConfiguration` for a `maxConcurrency` of 0 (`ComputeProviderForwardingTests.hintedDefaultsReachHintlessWitnesses`).

evidence.limitations: Pinned at the protocol-extension level with a hint-less-only conformer; the optimized search routes pass minChunk, so they take the same defaults, but no route-level test installs such a conformer.
